---
title: "`cd` — Cao–Dowd synthetic control with spillovers"
subtitle: "Single treated unit, fixed exposure structure, and end-of-sample inference"
---

`method="cd"` implements [Cao and Dowd (arXiv:1902.07343v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07343v3).
It fits an intercept and simplex synthetic-control weights for **every** unit
using pre-treatment outcomes. The researcher supplies a set of potentially
exposed units or a labeled, fixed structure matrix $A$. The model permits a
different direct and spillover effect in each post-treatment period.

## Fit

```python
from scspill import SCSPILL
from scspill.data import load_california_cd

panel = load_california_cd(51)  # 50 states + DC; 1970–2000; post starts 1989
result = SCSPILL({**panel.config_kwargs(), "display_graphs": False}).fit()
result.effects_panel.loc[1990, ["CA", "NV"]]
result.effect_ci["CA"].loc[1990]
```

The existing `load_california()` is a different 39-state, 1988-onward case
study and does not reproduce this paper. `load_california_cd(41)` supplies
the paper's reduced specification.

For a custom panel, pass `method="cd"`, `df`, `outcome`, `treat`, `unitid`,
`time`, and either `affected_units` or `spillover_structure="custom"` with a
pandas `effect_matrix`. The treatment flag is 1 only for the single treated
unit from the first post period onward. The `effect_matrix` rows must cover
every unit by label, and the treated unit's row must be its own direct-effect
indicator: a single 1, in a column that is zero for every other unit. Other columns may encode shared or
heterogeneous spillovers. All columns of $(I-\widehat B)A$ must be linearly
independent; the fit raises an identification error otherwise.

Writing $R=I-\widehat B$, the period-specific effect is

$$
\widehat\alpha_t=A[(RA)'(RA)]^{-1}(RA)'(RY_t-\widehat a).
$$

## Inference

The defaults are the paper's Section 4 definitions. The authors' Proposition
99 application code departs from them in two places, each kept as a switch
so its published numbers can be reproduced; see [Caveats](#caveats).

`result.test_hypothesis(C, d=0, period=1990)` tests a general linear
restriction $C\alpha_t=d$ by the squared P statistic. `C` can be a labeled
DataFrame or a matrix in `result.unit_labels` order. Identity and inverse
projected second-moment weights are available. Set
`reference_mode="leave_one_period_out"` to refit all SCM equations for each
held-out pre-treatment period; `"full"` is the paper's Section 4 definition
and the default.

`result.effect_ci[unit]` is the pointwise interval selected by `ci_method`.
Both versions are always stored: `pointwise_ci` (the default, the inverse of
the squared P test) and `published_ci` (the authors' application code).
`pointwise_p_values` holds the period-wise P values, and
`kappa_test[period]` checks the assumed structure $A$ period by period
(Section 5.1.2). `att` is the arithmetic mean of the post-period direct
estimates; no ATT confidence interval is implied by the pointwise intervals.

## Caveats {#caveats}

The authors' application code and the paper's stated procedure differ in
two places. `cd` follows the paper by default; each difference has a switch
that reproduces the application code. Leave-one-period-out references are a
third option.

| # | Paper, Section 4 (default) | Authors' application code | Switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Critical value $\inf\{x:\widehat F(x)\ge 1-\tau\}$, the left inverse of the empirical CDF | NumPy's linearly interpolated quantile | `quantile_method="linear"` |
| 2 | Intervals by inverting the squared P test, which makes them symmetric about $\widehat\alpha$ | $\widehat\alpha + [q_{\tau/2},\, q_{1-\tau/2}]$ of the signed pre-treatment errors $e_i'\widehat G\widehat u_t$ | `ci_method="published"` |
| 3 | Full-sample references | Full-sample references | `reference_mode="leave_one_period_out"` refits without each pre-treatment period |

What each one changes in practice:

1. With only 19 pre-treatment periods the two rules pick different order
   statistics. The paper's 95% critical value is
   $\lceil 0.95 \times 19 \rceil = 19$th, the largest reference statistic,
   so it rejects only when the post-treatment statistic exceeds all 19. The
   interpolated quantile sits at position 18.1, just above the second
   largest. In the 51-unit application the joint test for any spillover
   rejects in 1990–1992 and 1994–2000 under the application code's rule. In
   1994 and 1995 the statistic (1745.8 and 1725.3) lies between the
   interpolated cut-off (1482.8) and the largest reference value (1828.9),
   so the paper's definition does not reject, and the paper's own P value,
   $\#\{\widehat P_t \ge P\}/19 = 0.053$, is above 0.05.
2. Since $\widehat\alpha-\alpha\approx Gu_{T+1}$, a percentile interval for
   $\alpha$ subtracts the quantiles, $[\widehat\alpha-q_{1-\tau/2},\,
   \widehat\alpha-q_{\tau/2}]$. The published interval adds them, which
   agrees with that only when the error distribution is symmetric; for
   California in 1989 it gives $[-3.87, 3.27]$ where the subtracting form
   gives $[-3.11, 4.04]$. In the authors' repository the Proposition 99
   code (`run_spec.py` computes the quantiles, `make_figures.py` plots
   `te + lo` to `te + hi`) adds, while their continuous-treatment
   application (`continuous_treatment.m`) subtracts.
3. Leave-one-period-out references, an option the paper mentions (after
   Andrews 2003) rather than its definition, widen the intervals substantially in the
   California application; for California itself the range of the
   reference errors more than doubles.

The authors' own studies are not uniform either: their Monte Carlo size and
power studies and the $\kappa_A$ study use the left-inverse critical value
(`quantile_method="empirical"`), and the repository's README notes that its
confidence intervals were checked against the original MATLAB output only
for the point estimates.

## Reproducing the paper

The bundled panel is the input of the [authors' replication
package](https://github.com/jcao0/synthetic-control-spillover) at commit
`86004020`. The authors' application-code settings reproduce their published
numbers:

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scspill import SCSPILL
from scspill.data import load_california_cd

fit = SCSPILL(
    {
        **load_california_cd(51).config_kwargs(),
        "quantile_method": "linear",   # the authors' application code
        "ci_method": "published",
        "display_graphs": False,
    }
).fit()

# Estimate, 95% interval and P value for CA (direct) and NV, AZ, OR
table_s6 = pd.concat(
    {
        unit: fit.effect_ci[unit].assign(
            estimate=fit.effects_panel[unit], p_value=fit.pointwise_p_values[unit]
        )
        for unit in ["CA", "NV", "AZ", "OR"]
    },
    axis=1,
).round(2)

# Years in which "no spillover anywhere" is rejected
no_spill = np.eye(len(fit.unit_labels))[1:]
[t for t in fit.effects_panel.index if fit.test_hypothesis(no_spill, period=t).reject]

# California's synthetic-control weights and intercept
fit.scm_matrix.loc["CA"].nlargest(10), fit.intercepts["CA"]
```

`load_california_cd(41)` gives the paper's 41-unit robustness specification.
`scspill/tests/test_cd.py` checks both fits against the authors' saved
output: P values match exactly, and effects agree to within 0.01 packs.
The remaining gap is the simplex solver. With the authors' settings, SciPy's
SLSQP stops short of the optimum for every unit of the 51-unit panel; `cd`
uses scaled objectives with analytic gradients and reaches an objective at
or below theirs for every unit, so a few published two-decimal values
differ in the last digit.

Multiple treated units, covariates, time-varying $A$, and alternative
estimators are outside this implementation.
